hints.content:
Based on the second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus, $g$ is an antiderivative of $f$:

$g'=f$

This table summarizes the relationship between various properties of a function $f$ and its antiderivative $g$:

When the function $f$ is... | The antiderivative $g=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is...
:-: | :-:
Positive $+$ | Increasing $\nearrow$
Negative $-$ | Decreasing $\searrow$
Increasing $\nearrow$ | Concave up $\cup$
Decreasing $\searrow$ | Concave down $\cap$
Changes sign / crosses the $x$-axis | Extremum point
Extremum point | Inflection point

This is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ has a relative maximum at $x=c$:

$f$ crosses the $x$-axis from above it to below it.

The curve starts on the positive y-axis, moves downward concave down to (c, 0), continues downward concave up, and ends in quadrant 4. ](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/d35c43412e9a3097481adbd3ddd79ae7a407b11b)

Let $g(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.

**What is an appropriate calculus-based justification for the fact that $g$ has a relative maximum at $x=c$?**

[[☃ radio 1]]

choices.clue: It's true that $f$ has to be decreasing for $g$ to have a relative maximum point, but this is not enough. $f$ is decreasing at other points and $g$ doesn't have a relative maximum at each of these points.

choices.content: $f$ crosses the $x$-axis from above it to below it.

choices.clue: While it is true that when $f$ has a relative extremum, $g$ has an inflection point, the other direction isn't necessarily true. $f$ having an inflection point doesn't mean its antiderivative has an extremum point.
